questions.question_text: Nalmefene (Selincro) is approved in the EU for alcohol use disorder using a 'targeted' dosing strategy. How does its mechanism differ from naltrexone?

options.text: Nalmefene is a pure opioid antagonist; naltrexone is a partial agonist
Nalmefene is a mixed opioid antagonist/partial kappa agonist; naltrexone is a pure antagonist at all opioid receptors
Nalmefene acts on dopamine D3 receptors; naltrexone acts on mu receptors only
They have identical mechanisms but different routes of administration
Nalmefene blocks serotonin 5-HT3 receptors; naltrexone blocks opioid receptors

correct_answer.text: Nalmefene is a mixed opioid antagonist/partial kappa agonist; naltrexone is a pure antagonist at all opioid receptors

questions.explanation: Nalmefene is a mixed opioid receptor modulator: mu (μ) and delta (δ) antagonism, plus kappa (κ) partial agonism. Naltrexone is a non-selective pure antagonist at μ, δ, and κ opioid receptors. Nalmefene's kappa partial agonism may modulate the dysphoric/stress response component of cravings (KOR signalling mediates stress-induced relapse), providing additional anti-craving benefit beyond pure mu antagonism. Both agents reduce alcohol consumption by blocking opioid-mediated reward in the mesolimbic pathway. Nalmefene is approved in the EU for 'as-needed' targeted use — taken 1-2 hours before anticipated drinking occasions, allowing flexible use without daily dosing. This is distinct from naltrexone (daily oral or monthly depot IM) and acamprosate (daily oral). The ESENSE trials demonstrated significant reduction in heavy drinking days. NICE recommends nalmefene as an adjunct to psychosocial support in AUD patients who have high drinking risk levels and do not require immediate detoxification.

Reliability speaks to the consistency of a test such as from one test administration to another (testretest) or between different people administering the test (interrater). questions.question_text: Among the following, which is considered to be the most significant therapeutic factor in group psychotherapy?

options.text: Expression of emotion and cathartic release of tensions

questions.explanation: Cohesion is the sense that the group is working together towards a common goal. This is believed to be the most important factor related to positive therapeutic effects. Group cohesion has been likened to the therapeutic alliance in dyadic treatment. In dynamic therapies, specifi c and non-specifi c elements contribute to therapeutic change. In groups, the presence of other people adds to factors present in all dyadic healing relationships. Non-specifi c factors are embedded in the relationships established through a consistent, accepting, non-judgemental, and supportive environment. These are all elements of a cohesive group. Groups provide a corrective emotional experience in which patients experience others (including the therapist) responding to them differently from those in their past. Members share their stories (catharsis) and feel less isolated when others have shared similar stories (universalization); they have opportunities to be helpful to others through both cognitive understanding and emotional linking (imparting information, providing feedback, and altruism). They also see others improve, which conveys hope. These elements contribute to the sense of collaboration and a willingness to adopt norms (i.e. discuss feelings about the interactions in the meeting) that further members’ sense of effi cacy and belonging. They contribute to an experience of support and acceptance, which may be suffi cient therapeutic gain for a number of patients. Fight/fl ight, pairing, and dependency are Bion’s basic group assumptions that lead to a negative therapeutic effect. Tasman A, Maj M, First MB, et al. Psychiatry, 3rd edn. WileyBlackwell, 2007, p. 1908.

questions.question_text: Buprenorphine is widely used for opioid use disorder maintenance treatment. Its 'ceiling effect' on respiratory depression (at high doses) is explained by which pharmacological property?

options.text: High plasma protein binding preventing free drug accumulation
Partial agonism at mu-opioid receptors — plateau effect at high doses
Rapid CYP3A4 metabolism limiting plasma levels
Antagonism at delta-opioid receptors opposing respiratory effects
CNS P-glycoprotein efflux limiting brain penetration

correct_answer.text: Partial agonism at mu-opioid receptors — plateau effect at high doses

questions.explanation: Buprenorphine is a high-affinity partial agonist at mu-opioid receptors (MOR). As a partial agonist, its dose-response curve plateaus at submaximal efficacy — even at very high doses, it does not produce the same degree of respiratory depression as full agonists (heroin, morphine, oxycodone). This ceiling effect on respiratory depression is the key safety advantage over full opioid agonists for maintenance therapy. However, the ceiling effect applies only when pure buprenorphine is used; combining it with benzodiazepines or alcohol can overcome this protection (full respiratory depression possible). Buprenorphine also has: high receptor affinity (displacing full agonists — precipitating withdrawal if given before adequate washout); long half-life (~24-60h); slow receptor dissociation (blocking street opioid effects even if misused — 'blockade'). Naloxone is combined in Suboxone (4:1 buprenorphine:naloxone) to deter injection misuse (naloxone has poor oral bioavailability but blocks opioid effects if injected).

questions.question_text: Jack has certain core beliefs about being unlovable. He thinks that this characteristic makes people abandon him. In order to avoid this, he turns out to be excessively self-sacrifi cing to his family. From a schema-based treatment point of view, what is the underlying cognitive process that is maintaining the schema?
questions.explanation: Schema-based approaches in cognitive therapy are based on the original ideas of Beck. Early life experiences produce a number of thought patterns or schemata. These thought patterns are like ‘block moulds’ into which thoughts fi t in when evaluating events. They are otherwise called core beliefs. These result in underlying ‘assumptions’ which reinforce the core beliefs and from these arise the negative automatic thoughts. Schemata are thought to be dormant, and get activated during a depressive episode. Schemata are patterns of unconditional beliefs that are hard to access and are self-maintaining. There are thought to be three main processes that maintain schemata. Schema surrender is the process where the person seeks evidence that supports the beliefs and dismisses any evidence to the contrary. Schema compensation refers to compensating for the core belief by doing the exact opposite, but, ultimately, this action acts as a reinforcer that maintains the schema, as in the case described in the question. Ultimately, the person believes that the family loves him only because he is self-sacrifi cing, and if he was not, he would still remain unlovable. Schema avoidance is a group of blocking behaviours that help avoid emotional arousal – e.g. comfort eating. Naismith J and Grant S. Seminars in the Psychotherapies. Gaskell, 2007, p. 149.

Berne defi ned psychological ‘games’ as stereotyped and predictable transactions that people learn in childhood and continue to play throughout their lives. Strokes, the basic motivating factors of human behaviour consist of specifi c rewards such as approval and love. All people have three ego states that exist within them: the child (the primitive element), the adult (the reality element), and the parent (an introject of the values of a person’s actual parents). The therapeutic process helps people to understand whether they are functioning in a child, adult or parent mode when interacting with others. It is thought that as patients learn to recognize characteristic games being repeated throughout life, they can ultimately function in the adult mode as much as possible in interpersonal relationships. questions.question_text: The effectiveness of an clinical measure is measured by using pragmatic trials. Which trial design is normally employed when carrying out a pragmatic trial?
questions.explanation: RCTs provide high-quality evidence for or against proposed interventions. But RCTs have a major limitation in terms of generalizability. This is because the trials are conducted in a somewhat artifi cial experimental setting that is different from clinical practice. So RCTs have high internal validity due to rigorous methodology but poor external validity. Pragmatic RCTs are a type of RCTs introduced with the intention of increasing external validity, i.e. generalizability of RCT results. But this takes place at the expense of internal validity. questions.explanation: N-of-1 trials are randomized double-blind multiple crossover comparisons of an active drug against placebo in a single patient. correct_answer.text: The risk is higher in females across the life span.

At least some of the increased risk for PTSD in females appears to be attributable to a greater likelihood of exposure to traumatic events, such as rape, and other forms of interpersonal violence. Within populations exposed specifically to such stressors, gender differences in risk for PTSD are attenuated or nonsignificant.

questions.question_text: According to the evidence hierarchy, expert opinion alone without supporting clinical studies would be classified as:

questions.question_text: A study is evaluating the effect of agomelatine on postnatal depression at a mother and baby unit. Which one of the following should be considered when assessing the internal validity of this study?

options.text: Benefi ts of agomelatine in major depression outside the postpartum period
The degree to which the subjects adhered to the study protocol
The cost of using agomelatine compared with standard care
Consistency of the reported outcome in comparison with previous studies
Benefi ts of agomelatine in postpartum depression when used at an outpatient service

correct_answer.text: The degree to which the subjects adhered to the study protocol

questions.explanation: Internal validity is the degree to which a study establishes the cause-and-effect relationship between the treatment and the observed outcome. External validity is the degree to which the results of a study becomes applicable outside the experimental setting in which the study was conducted. In other words, external validity refers to generalizability of study results while internal validity refers to rigorousness of the research method. The benefi t of agomelatine in different populations (choices A and E) refers to external validity; the cost of the drug and consistency of results obtained from different studies are related to applicability of the intervention in a clinical setting. Assessment of adherence to study protocol is one of many ways of analysing the quality of an intervention trial. Slack MK and Drugalis JR. Establishing the internal and external validity of experimental studies. American Journal of Health–Systems Pharm 2001; 58: 2173–2184.

questions.question_text: In the hierarchy of evidence, Which of the following study designs would typically yield Level IIa evidence?
questions.explanation:
Level IIa evidence comes from at least one controlled study without randomisation; a cohort study with a parallel non-exposed control group is the classic example, as it involves deliberate comparison without random allocation. 
Case-control studies are explicitly listed under Level III (\'non-experimental descriptive studies\') in standard evidence hierarchies. Qualitative studies and case series fall outside or at the bottom of this hierarchy (Level III–IV). A randomised controlled trial yields Level Ib (or Ia if part of a systematic review), not IIa.

Conversion of the study to a prospective design

The results are not statistically significant

correct_answer.text: There is a 95% probability that the true effect lies between 8-32%

questions.question_text: Among the following, which is not a goal of family treatment?

options.text: Establishing clarity about tasks and responsibilities of family members
Reducing tension and disagreements between family members
Decreasing distress in the member considered to be the individual

questions.explanation: Family therapy is mostly employed in child psychiatry settings, when problems have usually been identifi ed in a child’s behaviour, which has led the family to seek help. The aim of family therapy is to improve family functioning and so help the identifi ed patient. The goals of family therapy include (1) improved communications; (2) improved autonomy for each member; (3) improved agreement about roles; (4) reduced confl ict; (5) reduced distress in the member who is the patient. Family therapy developed from Ackerman’s work on psychodynamics of family and Bateson’s work on communication. Ackerman’s work led to the development of psychodynamic methods of treatment, while Bateson’s work led to the system’s approach. Minuchin developed further the system’s approach in the USA to form the structural family therapy method. Gelder M, Harrison P, and Cowen P. Shorter Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry, 5th edn. Oxford University Press, 2006, p. 611.

questions.question_text: A meta-analysis of five high-quality RCTs investigating an antidepressant's efficacy would be classified as:

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding PTSD is true?

options.text: Specific EEG changes occur in chronic PTSD
Previous history of neurotic illness precludes the development of PTSD features
PTSD symptoms usually occur within 6 months of the perceived trauma
Autonomic hyperarousal symptoms are usually rare

correct_answer.text: PTSD symptoms usually occur within 6 months of the perceived trauma

questions.explanation: PTSD symptoms usually occur within 6 months of the perceived trauma. The essential features are autonomic hyperarousal, re-experiencing of aspects of the stressful event and active avoidance of cues that remind of the trauma. Anhedonia may also be seen; dramatic acute bursts of anxiety may present as exaggerated startle and hyperarousal. Insomnia is common. Predisposing factors include maladaptive personality traits (e.g. anankastic) or previous history of neurotic illnesses.

questions.question_text: In elderly patients started on standard antidepressants, which symptom typically improves last?
questions.explanation: Low mood or depressed mood is typically the last symptom to improve in elderly patients on antidepressants, while vegetative symptoms such as sleep, appetite, and anxiety improve within 1-2 weeks and energy/motivation improve within 4-6 weeks.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the unifying feature of the somatic symptom and related disorders category in DSM-5?

options.text: Excessive anxiety, preoccupation, or disproportionate behaviours related to somatic symptoms or health concerns
Voluntary production of symptoms motivated by external gain (e.g. financial, legal)
Presence of a clearly diagnosable general medical condition explaining all symptoms

questions.explanation: In DSM-5, the somatic symptom and related disorders category is unified by excessive and disproportionate thoughts, feelings, or behaviours related to somatic symptoms or health concerns  characterised by high levels of health anxiety and preoccupation with the body (Kaplan & Sadock\'s Synopsis, p.659). Crucially, DSM-5 removed the DSM-IV requirement that symptoms must lack a medical explanation (option E); a person may have a genuine medical condition and still receive a somatic symptom disorder diagnosis if their psychological response is disproportionate. Options B and D are irrelevant to this topic. Option C (\'denial of psychogenic cause\') is a clinical observation but is not the DSM-5 unifying criterion.

questions.question_text: A case vignette: An RCT of antipsychotic X vs. antipsychotic Y shows that antipsychotic X has a 20% absolute risk reduction in psychotic symptoms compared to antipsychotic Y. options.text: Apply the RCT findings directly to the 62-year-old patient without modification
Discard the RCT findings because the patient does not match the study population

Consider the RCT evidence valid but assess applicability by examining differences in age, comorbidities, and cognitive status; determine whether findings are likely to apply and consider patient preference
Use the RCT solely to guide diagnosis, not treatment decisions
Rely only on clinical experience without reference to the RCT

correct_answer.text: Consider the RCT evidence valid but assess applicability by examining differences in age, comorbidities, and cognitive status; determine whether findings are likely to apply and consider patient preference

questions.explanation: This scenario tests EBM integration: valid evidence (the RCT is high-quality Level I) must be judged for applicability to the specific patient. Evidence shows in Step 4: Patient preference and susceptibility to outcome needs to be assessed prior to application. The age difference, comorbidities, and cognitive status are clinically relevant factors affecting applicability. Option A ignores contextual differences. Option B dismisses valid evidence. Option D misuses the RCT. Option E abandons evidence-based practice. ---

Inability to measure incidence and reliance on odds ratio rather than relative risk
Lack of comparison group for analysis
Inability to study multiple exposures simultaneously
Poor suitability for investigating rare outcomes

correct_answer.text: Inability to measure incidence and reliance on odds ratio rather than relative risk

Option A describes cohort studies. Option C is incorrect as case-control studies require controls. Option D is false; case-control studies can study multiple etiological factors. questions.explanation: The critical issue here is applicability—whether the valid and impactful results can be applied to this specific patient given differences in demographics, age, gender, and socioeconomic status. options.text: Because volunteers always have the condition being studied
Because response rates can be very low, and those responding may differ significantly from non-responders
Because cross-sectional studies require large sample sizes
Because volunteers always provide accurate information

correct_answer.text: Because response rates can be very low, and those responding may differ significantly from non-responders

questions.explanation: The source lists Volunteer bias – as response rates can be very low as a limitation of cross-sectional studies. questions.question_text: MDMA (3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine)-assisted therapy is in Phase 3 trials for PTSD. MDMA's primary pharmacological mechanism involves:
questions.explanation: MDMA is a substrate for the serotonin (SERT), dopamine (DAT), and noradrenaline (NET) reuptake transporters. Rather than blocking these transporters competitively, MDMA enters the presynaptic terminal and reverses transporter direction, causing non-vesicular, calcium-independent release of monoamines into the synapse. Serotonin release dominates (approximately 3:1 ratio over dopamine), producing the characteristic prosocial, empathogenic, and anxiolytic effects that underpin its therapeutic utility in PTSD therapy. MDMA also releases oxytocin from the hypothalamus, inhibits amygdala reactivity to threat, and enhances extinction learning — which may be the therapeutic mechanism in PTSD; enhanced fear extinction during therapy sessions combined with increased trust and therapeutic alliance. The MAPS Phase 3 trials showed clinically and statistically significant PTSD symptom reduction with MDMA-AT vs placebo+therapy. MDMA is not a classic psychedelic (it lacks significant 5-HT2A agonism) and does not typically cause hallucinations.

questions.question_text: According to ICD-11, ADHD diagnosis requires evidence of symptoms prior to what age?
questions.explanation: ICD-11 ADHD diagnosis requires evidence of significant inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms prior to age 12, typically by early to mid-childhood, though clinical attention may come later.

Which of the following would benefit Mr. Thurston the most in relation to his PTSD and sleep disturbance?

options.text: Increasing the length of stage 3 and 4 sleep
Increasing the number of non-REM sleep cycles
Reducing the amount of waking from REM sleep

questions.explanation: REM sleep disruption is implicated in PTSD, mediated by sympathetic system over-activity. questions.question_text: A 24-week RCT of memantine in moderate–severe Alzheimer’s dementia was reported. The investigators recruited 126 subjects for the memantine arm and 126 for the placebo arm, out of which 100 in the memantine group and 100 in the placebo group completed the study. Using a categorical measure of treatment response it was shown that 40% of the individuals in the memantine group responded while only 20% in placebo group showed a response. Calculate the relative risk reduction of using memantine
questions.explanation: Relative risk reduction (or relative benefi t increase) is calculated using the following expression: relative risk reduction = absolute risk reduction/control event rate (RRR = ARR/ CER) The control event rate is 20%; the experimental event rate is 40%. Absolute risk reduction is the difference between the two event rates, i.e. 40 – 20 = 20% RRR = 20/20 = 1 Guyatt G and Rennie D, eds. Users’ Guides to the Medical Literature. A Manual for Evidence-based Clinical Practice. AMA Press, 2002, p. 660.

Since both paper A and paper B test the same construct (theoretical knowledge base of psychiatric trainees), examining the association between them tests convergent validity.

questions.explanation: Several synthetic and semisynthetic opioids are not detected on routine urine toxicology screening. For instance, fentanyl, buprenorphine, and methadone require assays for these substances in particular given structural differences relative to naturally occurring opioids (i.e., opiates), including morphine and codeine. Of note, all agents that activate mu receptors are known as opioids (literally, “resembling opiates”), and agonists that are structurally related to compounds derived from opium poppy are opiates proper. The DSM5 uses the more encompassing term opioid, as in “opioid use disorder” and “opioid withdrawal.”

questions.question_text: Which of the following antidementia drugs acts directly on nicotine receptors?
questions.explanation: Galantamine, unlike the other anticholinesterases in clinical use, is derived from the alkaloids from the daffodil and snowdrop family. It is a reversible, competitive inhibitor of acetylcholinesterase with some inhibitory action on butyrylcholinesterase. It is also an agonist at nicotinic receptor sites. Although a clinically effective drug, galantamine frequently causes gastrointestinal side effects.

questions.question_text: A woman maintained on paroxetine throughout pregnancy delivers a baby. What is a recognized complication of paroxetine use in late pregnancy?
questions.explanation: SSRI use in late pregnancy, particularly paroxetine, is associated with persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN) and neonatal adaptation syndrome.

questions.question_text: A trial is conducted to evaluate the effi cacy of lamotrigine in individuals with symptoms of recurrent depersonalization. While calculating the number of individuals needed in the trial to demonstrate a meaningful effect, α level is set at 0.05. Which of the following is true regarding alpha (α)?

options.text: It is the probability of a type 2 error
It is the threshold for defi ning clinical signifi cance
If α = 0.05, there is a 5% chance that the null hypothesis is rejected wrongly
If α = 0.05, then 5% of treated subjects will show absence of treatment effect.

correct_answer.text: If α = 0.05, there is a 5% chance that the null hypothesis is rejected wrongly

questions.explanation: Α is the probability of type 1 error. It is used to set the threshold for statistical (not clinical) signifi cance, often arbitrarily set as p = 0.01–0.05 (α = 1–5%). If α = 0.05, there is a 1 in 20 or 5% chance that the null hypothesis is rejected wrongly. Lawrie SM, McIntosh AM, and Rao S. Critical Appraisal for Psychiatry. Churchill Livingstone, 2000, p. 64.

questions.question_text: While adapting the results of an RCT into clinical practice, a clinician wants to calculate the new NNT values for his own clinical population using the results of the RCT. Apart from the reported RCT which of the following is needed to carry out the calculation of the new NNT?

options.text: The expected rate of spontaneous resolution of the treated condition in the clinical population
The size of the clinical population
The case fatality rate for the treated condition in the clinical population
Lifetime prevalence of the disease in the clinical population

correct_answer.text: The expected rate of spontaneous resolution of the treated condition in the clinical population

questions.explanation: Published RCTs may quote impressive outcomes in terms of NNT. Applying principles of evidence-based medicine, one must check for the internal validity of a study and the degree of generalizability before adapting the results to clinical practice. One must also be aware of the fact that though clinically more meaningful, NNTs quoted in RCTs may not translate to the same extent in actual clinical practice. One way of appreciating the usefulness of a newly introduced drug is to calculate the NNT for one’s own clinical population (target population). To enable this one may estimate the patient expected event rate (PEER), which is given by the expected spontaneous resolution rate or the response rate for an existing standard treatment. This can be obtained from the local audit data or clinical experience. The product of PEER and relative benefi t increase from the published RCT gives the new absolute benefi t increase (ABI new) value for the target population. The inverse of the new ABI gives the new NNT for the target population. The disease prevalence rate or absolute size of the target population has no effect on the new NNT. Lawrie SM, McIntosh AM, Rao S. Critical Appraisal for Psychiatry. Churchill Livingstone, 2000, p. 117.

questions.question_text: A shy 26yearold female patient has never been in a romantic relationship. After 5 months of psychodynamic treatment, she begins to struggle with strong positive feelings toward her male therapist, which she finds hard to accept. This occurs at the same time she is beginning to date someone from work. Her relationship with her colleague is likely an example of:
questions.explanation: Sometimes patients are not aware of their repressed feelings and express them as an action— as this patient is doing with her colleague. The action is repeated in an unconscious manner. For the therapist it is important to try to understand what is being communicated. Transference is generally defined as the set of expectations, beliefs, and emotional responses that a patient brings to the patient– doctor relationship, which are not necessarily based on who the doctor is or how the doctor acts in reality but, rather, on repeated experiences the patient has had with other important authority figures throughout life.

questions.question_text: Confi dence intervals are used to describe the range of uncertainty around the estimated value of an outcome from the sample studied. Which of the following statements about confi dence intervals is incorrect?

options.text: Sample size is used in calculating confi dence intervals
It includes a range of values above and below the point estimate
If the confi dence interval includes a null treatment effect, the null hypothesis can be rejected
95% confi dence interval is often used in clinical studies
When the estimated outcome is a ratio, a positive treatment effect is shown by confi dence intervals remaining above one.

correct_answer.text: If the confi dence interval includes a null treatment effect, the null hypothesis can be rejected

questions.explanation: If the confi dence interval includes a null treatment effect, the null hypothesis cannot be rejected within the set levels of confi dence limits. Confi dence intervals provide a measure of dispersion of the point estimate within stipulated confi dence limits (arbitrarily 95% corresponds to a p value of 5%). In other words, confi dence intervals provide the assured range within which the true value may lie. Confi dence intervals are a measure of precision of the results obtained from a study. The larger the sample studied, the narrower the intervals. If the confi dence intervals cross the value ‘0’ for the difference between means then the results are statistically not signifi cant. If it crosses the value ‘1’ for ratio measures such as the odds ratio, it is not signifi cant. If it crosses infi nity for inverse ratios such as NNT then it is not signifi cant. Johnstone EC, et al., eds. Companion to Psychiatric Studies, 7th edn. Churchill Livingstone, 2004, p. 192.

questions.question_text: Cue exposure therapy for substance use disorder involves:

Abnormal preoccupation with health and fear of having disease despite lack of physical evidence
Intentional production of false symptoms for external gain
Distress caused by recurrent intrusive thoughts

questions.explanation: Hypochondriasis (illness anxiety disorder in DSM-5) is characterized by abnormal preoccupation with one's health and a fear of having or getting a disease despite physical evidence to the contrary, as exemplified by the man convinced he had cancer.

Well-conducted clinical studies without RCTs or extrapolated from Level I
Expert committee reports and opinion only

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old man who works for the state as a highway and bridge designer becomes extremely anxious when he has to drive across any bridge. Which technique can best help him?
questions.explanation: Systematic desensitization can reduce anxiety in a situation by identifying a hierarchy of situations that produce anxiety from low to high. For example, the bridge designer can be taught progressive muscle relaxation until he is as relaxed as possible, at which point he will begin by driving across the shortest or least anxiety-producing bridge (in vivo exposure). As he successfully experiences crossing the lowest anxiety-producing bridge, he can proceed up the hierarchy of bridges until he masters crossing the most anxiety-producing bridge.

questions.question_text: Which characteristic of case-control studies makes them particularly unsuitable for studying exposures that are extremely common in a population?

options.text: Common exposures create a ceiling effect that masks associations
When exposure is common, cases and controls will have similar exposure rates, reducing the exposure contrast needed to detect differences
Common exposures cannot be measured retrospectively
Controls cannot be selected from exposed populations
The odds ratio becomes unreliable when exposure prevalence exceeds 50%

correct_answer.text: When exposure is common, cases and controls will have similar exposure rates, reducing the exposure contrast needed to detect differences

questions.explanation: Case-control studies are useful when exposure is common but disease is rare. The complementary weakness (not stated but implied) is when both exposure and disease are common—the contrast between case and control exposure rates diminishes, reducing the ability to detect differences. This is the fundamental logic: case-control studies need sufficient variation between groups to demonstrate associations. When everyone in both groups has the exposure, no difference can be detected. This is distinct from measurement reliability or technical limits of the odds ratio.

questions.question_text: Sodium oxybate (gamma-hydroxybutyrate, GHB) is approved for narcolepsy with cataplexy. Its mechanism relevant to both cataplexy treatment and its abuse potential involves:

options.text: GHB/GABA-B receptor agonism producing deep sleep architecture consolidation
Adenosine A2A receptor blockade in the basal ganglia
Dopamine transporter blockade in the mesolimbic pathway

correct_answer.text: GHB/GABA-B receptor agonism producing deep sleep architecture consolidation

questions.explanation: Sodium oxybate (GHB) acts primarily as a GHB receptor agonist (at GHB-specific receptors, distinct from GABA receptors) and, at higher concentrations, as a GABA-B receptor agonist. Its therapeutic benefit in narcolepsy with cataplexy stems from: improving nocturnal sleep architecture (increasing slow-wave sleep, reducing fragmentation, and consolidating right-time sleep) → reducing daytime sleepiness and cataplexy attacks. The mechanism of anti-cataplexy action likely involves normalising REM sleep regulation and reducing the REM intrusions into wakefulness that characterise narcolepsy. Abuse potential: GHB is a CNS depressant with euphoric effects at recreational doses; rapid onset (15-30 min) and amnestic properties also make it a drug-of-misuse. It was banned in many countries before re-emerging as a controlled prescription drug. New low-sodium oxybate (Lumryz) formulations reduce sodium load risk. Pitolisant (H3 inverse agonist) is a newer alternative for narcolepsy with a different mechanism.

questions.question_text: A patient expressing, “cabbages to kings” during a therapy session is a good example of which fundamental technique in psychoanalysis?
questions.explanation: Free association is a predominant technique in psychoanalysis. The fundamental rule of free association is for the patient to tell the analysis everything that comes to their mind, the unimportant and nonsensical, and it does not mirror normal conversation.

questions.question_text: A clinical trial uses intention-to-treat analysis. What is the main advantage of ITT analysis?
questions.explanation: Intention-to-treat analysis analyzes all participants as randomized regardless of adherence, maintaining the benefits of randomization and avoiding selection bias.

questions.question_text: A researcher suspects that sleep deprivation increases the risk of depressive episode onset. To test this hypothesis by prospectively following sleep-deprived and non-sleep-deprived adolescents over 3 years and measuring subsequent depression diagnosis, which study design is most appropriate?

options.text: Case-control study of past sleep patterns

questions.explanation: According to NESARC (Grant et al., 2004), around 29% of individuals meeting criteria for alcohol dependence also satisfy DSM-IV criteria for major depressive disorder in the past 12 months, making C the correct answer.
